# The last night

My last night shift was on Saturday: 9pm to 7.30am in majors. Fourteen years of nights, and then, at half past seven on a Sunday morning, I handed over and went home.

I thought I knew how I would feel. My knees have been making their views on the rota known for some time, my sleep is a mess, and my GP recently informed me that my blood pressure is not a joke anymore. The move to days only, starting Monday, is sensible. I am relieved about it.

I also feel a little like a traitor for being relieved.

This isn’t going to be another post about staffing. I’ve written enough of those, and this isn’t quite that. It’s about leaving a way of working that has shaped most of my adult life as a doctor, and discovering that even a change you need can feel like a loss.

I worked my first night as an SHO in 2012. I remember how strange it felt to walk into the hospital when the rest of the city was settling down, and how much stranger it felt to come out in the morning and find everyone else beginning their day. For years afterwards, I would occasionally forget that other people didn’t live this way. That a Tuesday morning was not, for most of Leicester, the middle of the night.

During my first winter of nights, I cried in the car park at the Infirmary because I couldn’t remember whether I had given a second dose. I had. But I can still remember sitting there with frost on the windscreen, trying to work out whether I had got something wrong.

I would like to say that fourteen years made me certain of everything. They didn’t. They did teach me to check, to ask someone else to check when I needed them to, and to recognise that there were colleagues around me doing the same careful work, even when we were all tired.

People tend to think nights in emergency medicine are about adrenaline. Sometimes they are. Mostly, I think, they are about staying kind at five in the morning when you are empty. Listening to someone who has already told their story several times. Explaining something again without letting your tiredness become their problem. Finding a chair, or a blanket, or a few more minutes when there don’t seem to be any.

Last winter, an old gentleman held my hand at around three in the morning and told me I had his daughter’s hands. He went home three days later. I still think about that sometimes. There was nothing particularly medical about the moment, but it has stayed with me alongside everything else I learned to do on nights.

There is kindness among staff, too. I think nights are where the department is most itself. There are fewer managers around, and perhaps because of that—or perhaps because it’s three in the morning and nobody has the energy to pretend—there is more honesty. People will tell you when they’re worried. Someone will notice you haven’t stopped. Someone else will quietly take over a task because they can see you need a minute.

And at four, somebody makes toast in the staff room. It happens with such regularity that it ought to be on the rota, but nobody ever admits to starting it. You walk in and there it is. I have never got to the bottom of who puts the first slice in, and after all this time I’ve decided I don’t need to know.

Nights have taken things, of course. My knees and my sleep, for a start. They’ve made ordinary plans complicated and turned days off into a kind of negotiation with my own body. I missed both my nieces’ naming ceremonies over video because of nights. My sister in Bangalore never once complained, which somehow makes me feel worse about it, not better. There are things I can make more time for now, but I can’t go back and be present for those particular mornings.

So I’m trying not to make the last shift into a grand farewell. It was a shift in majors, with work to do and a handover at the end. The fact that it was my last one didn’t make me any less tired, or make the decision to leave nights any less necessary.

On Sunday morning I drove home down the London Road as the sun was coming up, listening to the Shipping Forecast on catch-up. Somewhere along the way I realised I would not see that light from this side again: the particular light you drive into after everyone else has started waking up and you are finally going to bed. I’ll see plenty of mornings on the days rota, but they won’t be quite the same.

I’m glad about that. I’m sad about it too. Both seem to be true, and I’m going to stop trying to make them cancel each other out.

Folasade, our charge nurse on nights, has been doing them for twenty-two years and still beats me up the stairs. She’ll be there when the department settles into another night, and, at four in the morning, there will almost certainly be toast. Nobody will admit to making it.
